statement: Given two spheres about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.
heath_proof: Let two spheres be conceived about the same centre A; thus it is required to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface. Let the spheres be cut by any plane through the centre; then the sections will be circles, inasmuch as the sphere was produced by the diameter remaining fixed and the semicircle being carried round it; [XI. Def. 14] hence, in whatever position we conceive the semicircle to be, the plane carried through it will produce a circle on the circumference of the sphere. And it is manifest that this circle is the greatest possible, inasmuch as the diameter of the sphere, which is of course the diameter both of the semicircle and of the circle, is greater than all the straight lines drawn across in the circle or the sphere. Let then BCDE be the circle in the greater sphere, and FGH the circle in the lesser sphere; let two diameters in them, BD, CE, be drawn at right angles to one another; then, given the two circles BCDE, FGH about the same centre, let there be inscribed in the greater circle BCDE an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle FGH, let BK, KL, LM   ME be its sides in the quadrant BE. let KA be joined and carried through to N, let AO be set up from the point A at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE, and let it meet the surface of the sphere at O, and through AO and each of the straight lines BD, KN let planes be carried; they will then make greatest circles on the surface of the sphere, for the reason stated. Let them make such, and in them let BOD, KON be the semicircles on BD, KN. Now, since OA is at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE, therefore all the planes through OA are also at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE; [XI. 18] hence the semicircles BOD, KON are also at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE. And, since the semicircles BED, BOD, KON are equal, for they are on the equal diameters BD, KN, therefore the quadrants BE, BO, KO are also equal to one another. Therefore there are as many straight lines in the quadrants BO, KO equal to the straight lines BK, KL, LM, ME as there are sides of the polygon in the quadrant BE. Let them be inscribed, and let them be BP, PQ, QR, RO and KS, ST, TU, UO, let SP, TQ, UR be joined, and from P, S let perpendiculars be drawn to the plane of the circle BCDE; [XI. 11] these will fall on BD, KN, the common sections of the planes, inasmuch as the planes of BOD, KON are also at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE. [cf. XI. Def. 4] Let them so fall, and let them be PV, SW, and let WV be joined. Now since, in the equal semicircles BOD, KON, equal straight lines BP, KS have been cut off, and the perpendiculars PV, SW have been drawn, therefore PV is equal to SW, and BV to KW. [III. 27, I. 26] But the whole BA is also equal to the whole KA; therefore the remainder VA is also equal to the remainder WA; therefore, as BV is to VA, so is KW to WA; therefore WV is parallel to KB. [VI. 2] And, since each of the straight lines PV, SW is at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE, therefore PV is parallel to SW. [XI. 6] But it was also proved equal to it; therefore WV, SP are also equal and parallel. [I. 33] And, since WV is parallel to SP, while WV is parallel to KB, therefore SP is also parallel to KB. [XI. 9] And BP, KS join their extremities; therefore the quadrilateral KBPS is in one plane, inasmuch as, if two straight lines be parallel, and points be taken at random on each of them, the straight line joining the points is in the same plane with the parallels. [XI. 7] For the same reason each of the quadrilaterals SPQT, TQRU is also in one plane. But the triangle URO is also in one plane. [XI. 2] If then we conceive straight lines joined from the points P, S, Q, T, R, U to A, there will be constructed a certain polyhedral solid figure between the circumferences BO, KO, consisting of pyramids of which the quadrilaterals KBPS, SPQT, TQRU and the triangle URO are the bases and the point A the vertex. And, if we make the same construction in the case of each of the sides KL, LM, ME as in the case of BK, and further in the case of the remaining three quadrants, there will be constructed a certain polyhedral figure inscribed in the sphere and contained by pyramids, of which the said quadrilaterals and the triangle URO, and the others corresponding to them, are the bases and the point A the vertex. I say that the said polyhedron will not touch the lesser sphere at the surface on which the circle FGH is. Let AX be drawn from the point A perpendicular to the plane of the quadrilateral KBPS, and let it meet the plane at the point X; [XI. 11] let XB, XK be joined. Then, since AX is at right angles to the plane of the quadrilateral KBPS, therefore it is also at right angles to all the straight lines which meet it and are in the plane of the quadrilateral. [XI. Def. 3] Therefore AX is at right angles to each of the straight lines BX, XK. And, since AB is equal to AK, the square on AB is also equal to the square on AK. And the squares on AX, XB are equal to the square on AB, for the angle at X is right; [I. 47] and the squares on AX, XK are equal to the square on AK. [id.] Therefore the squares on AX, XB are equal to the squares on AX, XK. Let the square on AX be subtracted from each; therefore the remainder, the square on BX, is equal to the remainder, the square on XK; therefore BX is equal to XK. Similarly we can prove that the straight lines joined from X to P, S are equal to each of the straight lines BX, XK. Therefore the circle described with centre X and distance one of the straight lines XB, XK will pass through P, S also, and KBPS will be a quadrilateral in a circle. Now, since KB is greater than WV, while WV is equal to SP, therefore KB is greater than SP. But KB is equal to each of the straight lines KS, BP; therefore each of the straight lines KS, BP is greater than SP. And, since KBPS is a quadrilateral in a circle, and KB, BP, KS are equal, and PS less, and BX is the radius of the circle, therefore the square on KB is greater than double of the square on BX. Let KZ be drawn from K perpendicular to BV. Then, since BD is less than double of DZ, and, as BD is to DZ, so is the rectangle DB, BZ to the rectangle DZ, ZB, if a square be described upon BZ and the parallelogram on ZD be completed, then the rectangle DB, BZ is also less than double of the rectangle DZ, ZB. And, if KD be joined, the rectangle DB, BZ is equal to the square on BK, and the rectangle DZ, ZB equal to the square on KZ; [III. 31, VI. 8 and Por.] therefore the square on KB is less than double of the square on KZ. But the square on KB is greater than double of the square on BX; therefore the square on KZ is greater than the square on BX. And, since BA is equal to KA, the square on BA is equal to the square on AK. And the squares on BX, XA are equal to the square on BA, and the squares on KZ, ZA equal to the square on KA; [I. 47] therefore the squares on BX, XA are equal to the squares on KZ, ZA, and of these the square on KZ is greater than the square on BX; therefore the remainder, the square on ZA, is less than the square on XA. Therefore AX is greater than AZ; therefore AX is much greater than AG. And AX is the perpendicular on one base of the polyhedron, and AG on the surface of the lesser sphere; hence the polyhedron will not touch the lesser sphere on its surface. Therefore, given two spheres about the same centre, a polyhedral solid has been inscribed in the greater sphere which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.
ai_proof_text:
12.17
**Statement:** Given two spheres about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.

**Step 1.** Let A be the common centre of the two spheres. Every point of the surface of a sphere is at a distance from its centre equal to the radius of the generating semicircle [D11.14, D11.16]. Cut both spheres by any plane through A. In each sphere the section is a plane figure bounded by one line all of whose points are equally distant from A; hence each section is a circle with centre A [D1.15, D1.16]. Let the section of the greater sphere be the circle BCDE, that of the lesser the circle FGH, AB a radius of the greater, and G the point in which AB cuts the lesser circle, so that AG is a radius of the lesser sphere and AG < AB.

**Step 2.** Draw in the circle BCDE the diameter CE at right angles to the diameter BD [1.11], and let H be the point of the quadrant BE in which the straight line drawn through G at right angles to BD [1.11] meets the circle BCDE. By 12.16 inscribe in the greater circle BCDE an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle FGH, taking B as the end of the diameter BD used in that construction. The construction of 12.16 cuts off the side by bisecting continually the arc between the end B of the diameter and the point H (the point where the perpendicular to BD at its intersection G with the lesser circle meets the greater circle), until an arc less than the arc BH is left; the side is therefore a 2^n-th part of the circumference with n ≥ 3, and the vertex K next to B lies on the arc BH. Consequently the vertices of the polygon include B, C, D, E, and each quadrant contains a whole number m ≥ 2 of sides. Let BK, KL, LM, ME be the sides in the quadrant BE, and let s denote their common length.

**Step 3.** Join KA and produce it to N [P1, P2]. From A set up AX at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE [11.12], X being on the surface of the greater sphere. Draw the plane through AX and BD, and the plane through AX and KN; being planes through the centre A, their sections with the greater sphere are circles with centre A and radius AB (Step 1). Let BXD, KXN be the semicircles of these circles on the side of X. Since AX is at right angles to the plane BCDE, every plane through AX is at right angles to the plane BCDE [11.18]; hence the planes of BXD and KXN are at right angles to the plane BCDE.

**Step 4.** The circles BCDE, BXD, KXN have equal radii and are therefore equal [D3.1]. The angles BAE, BAX, KAX are right (Step 2; AX makes right angles with BA and KA which lie in the plane BCDE [D11.3]), hence equal [P4]; standing at the centres of equal circles they cut off equal arcs [3.26], so the arcs BX and KX are quadrants each equal to the quadrant BE. The quadrant BE is made up of the m arcs BK, KL, LM, ME, which are equal because they are cut off by equal chords [3.28]. Fit into the circle BXD, from B toward X, the chord BO equal to BK [4.1]; it cuts off the arc BO equal to the arc BK [3.28]. Continuing, fit OP, PR, RX each equal to BK, and in the circle KXN fit KS, ST, TU, UX each equal to BK. Since arc BX = arc KX = arc BE, and each is m times the arc BK, these m chords in each quadrant end exactly at X. Join SO, TP, UR [P1].

**Step 5.** In the plane BXD draw OV at right angles to BD [1.12], and in the plane KXN draw SQ at right angles to KN [1.12]. Since the planes BXD, KXN are at right angles to the plane BCDE, and BD, KN are their common sections with it, OV and SQ are at right angles to the plane BCDE [D11.4]. Moreover V falls between A and B: the angle BAO is less than the right angle BAX [CN5], the angle ABO is equal to it [1.5] and therefore acute, and if V lay beyond B (or beyond A), the acute angle ABO (or BAO) would be an exterior angle of the triangle OVB (or OVA), hence greater than the right angle at V [1.16], which is impossible. Likewise Q falls between A and K.

**Step 6.** The arcs BO, BK, KS are equal (Step 4), so the angles BAO, BAK, KAS at the centre are equal [3.27]. The triangles AVO, AQS have the angle OAV equal to the angle SAQ, right angles at V and Q, and the side AO equal to the side AS (radii); therefore OV = SQ and AV = AQ [1.26]. Since AB = AK, the remainders VB, QK are equal [CN3].

**Step 7.** Since BV = KQ and VA = QA, BV : VA = KQ : QA [5.7, 5.11]; therefore VQ is parallel to BK [6.2]. OV and SQ, being at right angles to the same plane, are parallel [11.6], and they are equal; hence VQ and OS are equal and parallel [1.33]. Since VQ is parallel to BK, OS is parallel to BK [11.9]. BO and KS join points on the parallels BK, OS, so they lie in the plane of BK and OS [11.7]; thus KBOS is a plane quadrilateral. In the same way, using the perpendiculars from P and T, and from R and U, to the plane BCDE, the straight lines TP and UR are each parallel to BK, so SO, TP, UR are parallel to one another [11.9], and the quadrilaterals SOPT, TPRU are plane [11.7]; the triangle URX is in one plane [11.2].

**Step 8.** Join AO, AS, AP, AT, AR, AU [P1]. Then on the bases KBOS, SOPT, TPRU, URX pyramids with vertex A are constructed [D11.12]. Make the same construction in the quadrants EC, CD, DB of the circle BCDE, and on the other side of the plane BCDE with AX produced through A. The pyramids so obtained make up a polyhedral solid contained by the plane quadrilaterals and triangles so formed, all of whose vertices lie on the surface of the greater sphere (each lies on a great circle of it); thus the solid is inscribed in the greater sphere. It remains to prove that no base of it touches the surface of the lesser sphere.

**Step 9.** From A draw AY perpendicular to the plane KBOS [11.11], Y being in that plane. AY makes right angles with YB, YK, YO, YS [D11.3], so AB² = AY² + YB², AK² = AY² + YK², AO² = AY² + YO², AS² = AY² + YS² [1.47]. Since AB = AK = AO = AS, the remainders YB², YK², YO², YS² are equal [CN3]; hence YB = YK = YO = YS.

**Step 10.** Since VQ is parallel to BK, the triangles AVQ, ABK are equiangular [1.29], so AV : AB = VQ : BK [6.4]; and AV < AB, hence VQ < BK [5.14]. But OS = VQ (Step 7). Therefore OS < s, while BK = BO = KS = s.

**Step 11.** The triangles YBK, YBO, YKS have YB = YK = YO = YS and bases BK = BO = KS, so the angles BYK, BYO, KYS are equal [1.8]. The triangles YOS, YBK have YO = YB, YS = YK and base OS less than base BK, so the angle OYS is less than the angle BYK [1.25]. Y lies within the quadrilateral KBOS: otherwise the four points B, K, S, O of the circle about centre Y would lie on one semicircle of it, and the angle at Y subtended by one side of the quadrilateral would be equal to or greater than the sum of the angles subtended by the other three sides, hence greater than each of them, which is impossible since three of the four angles are equal and the fourth is less than them. Therefore the four angles BYK, KYS, SYO, OYB about the point Y together make four right angles [1.15]. Thus three angles equal to BYK together with the angle OYS make four right angles, and OYS < BYK; so four angles equal to BYK exceed four right angles, and the angle BYK is greater than a right angle, i.e. obtuse [D1.11]. Hence in the triangle BYK, BK² > BY² + YK² = 2·BY² [2.12].

**Step 12.** From K draw KZ at right angles to BD [1.12]. As in Step 5, Z falls between A and B (the angle BAK is less than the right angle BAE [CN5], and the angle ABK is equal to it [1.5]). Join KD [P1]. The angle BKD, being in a semicircle, is right [3.31]; KZ is the perpendicular from the right angle to the base, so the triangles DBK, KBZ are similar and DB : BK = BK : BZ, and the triangles DZK, KZB are similar and DZ : ZK = ZK : ZB [6.8]; hence BK² = DB·BZ and KZ² = DZ·ZB [6.17].

**Step 13.** Since Z is between A and B, BZ < BA = AD < DZ. Now DB·BZ = DZ·ZB + BZ² [2.3]; and BZ², being the rectangle contained by BZ and ZB with BZ < DZ, is a part of the rectangle DZ·ZB and so less than it [CN5]. Therefore DB·BZ < 2·DZ·ZB, that is, BK² < 2·KZ².

**Step 14.** From Steps 11 and 13, 2·BY² < BK² < 2·KZ², so BY² < KZ² and BY < KZ. Since AB = AK, AB² = AK². But AB² = AY² + YB² (Step 9), and AK² = AZ² + ZK², the angle AZK being right [1.47]. Hence AY² + YB² = AZ² + ZK², and since YB² < ZK², AY² > AZ²; therefore AY > AZ.

**Step 15.** Since K lies on the arc BH (Step 2), the angle BAK is less than the angle BAH [CN5], so AK falls within the angle BAH and meets GH at a point W between G and H. In the right-angled triangle AGW, AW² = AG² + GW² < AG² + GH² = AH² [1.47, CN5]; so AW < AH = AK, and W lies between A and K. GW and ZK are both at right angles to AB, hence parallel [1.28]; so the straight line through W parallel to the side ZK of the triangle AZK cuts AZ at G, and, W being between A and K, G is between A and Z [6.2]. Therefore AZ > AG [CN5].

**Step 16.** Consequently AY > AZ > AG. Every straight line drawn from A to a point of the plane KBOS other than Y is greater than AY, since it makes with AY a right angle at Y [D11.3] and its square is AY² together with the square on the line joining Y to that point [1.47]. Hence every point of the base KBOS is at a distance from A greater than AG; but the surface of the lesser sphere consists of the points at distance AG from A [D11.14]. Therefore the base KBOS does not meet the surface of the lesser sphere.

**Step 17.** The same holds for every other base. Every quadrilateral base, such as SOPT, has two opposite sides (OP, TS) equal to s and the other two (SO, TP) less than s, TP being less than KL exactly as VQ is less than BK (Step 10); every triangular base, such as URX, has two sides (UX, RX) equal to s and the third (UR) less; and the bases in the other quadrants and on the other side of the plane BCDE are of these same two kinds. Let AY' be the perpendicular from A to such a base [11.11]. Then Y' is equidistant from the vertices of the base (as in Step 9), the angles at Y' subtended by the sides equal to s are equal [1.8], those subtended by the shorter sides are less than them [1.25], Y' lies within the base (as in Step 11), and the angles about Y' make four right angles [1.15]. Hence twice the angle subtended by a side equal to s, together with the smaller angle or angles, makes four right angles, so that angle is greater than a right angle, and by [2.12] s² > 2·Y'O², O being an end of a side equal to s. Then, as in Step 14, 2·Y'O² < s² < 2·KZ², so Y'O < KZ, and AY'² = AO² − Y'O² > AK² − KZ² = AZ² > AG² (Step 15). Thus AY' > AG, and, as in Step 16, the base lies wholly outside the surface of the lesser sphere.

**Step 18.** Therefore a polyhedral solid has been inscribed in the greater sphere which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface. Q.E.F.
